book.title: The Ahî Organization: Good Work and Good People (A1)

pages.title: A Group for Workers
pages.content:
Seven hundred years ago, there was a special group in Anatolia. Its name was the Ahî Organization. It was a group for workers and masters. The group helped workers in both work and daily life. This group taught people to be good and kind. At work, older workers taught new learners, and everyone worked well together.

It visited the shops and checked their work. It also checked things, chose good prices, and helped with work problems. When people had a problem, the Ahîs helped them. The organization was very important in the early years of the Ottomans, too.

vocabulary.definition: A big group of people with one job.
A person who does a job.
A person who is very good at a job.
Look at something carefully.
How much money something is.

pages.title: Good People
pages.content:
For the Ahîs, a good worker was also a good person. They were honest and never told lies. They were generous, so they helped poor people and visited sick neighbors. They did not do things that Allah does not want.

Young Ahîs learned good manners from their teachers, too. They learned to be nice to people everywhere, even in the street. For them, good work and a good heart always went together.

pages.title: Learning a Job
pages.content:
A young person started work as an apprentice. He worked in a shop next to a master. The master taught him the job day after day. After many years, the apprentice became a good worker. Later, he became a master, too.

For the Ahîs, bad work was a shame. So an apprentice could not open his own shop too early. First, his master had to say, “Now you are ready.” The Ahî shops were like schools. People learned a job there, and they also learned to be good people.

pages.title: Bad Shoes
pages.content:
There was a shoemaker in a small town. He wanted to earn more money. So he used cheap leather for his shoes. The shoes looked nice, but they were not strong.

People bought them. After only two or three weeks, the shoes were already broken. The customers were very angry. They went to the Ahî leader. “Look at these shoes!” they said. “They are new, but they are broken.”

pages.title: Shoes on the Roof
pages.content:
The Ahî leader went to the shop and looked at the shoes carefully. They really were bad. Then he took the shoes and threw them up on the roof of the shop!

Everybody in the town saw the shoes up there. Now they knew about the bad work. This was a warning for the shoemaker: “Make good shoes, or you cannot sell shoes in this town again.” In Turkish, people still say “pabucu dama atılmak”. It means “his shoes are on the roof”.

pages.title: Not Ready Yet
pages.content:
In a town in Anatolia, a young Ahî learner made nice things from glass with his master. One day, he said, “My master, I think I am ready to open my own shop.” But his master answered, “You are not ready yet.”

The young learner did not listen. He moved to a different city and opened a shop there. He made glass cups. But after a short time, all the cups broke. Nobody wanted his cups, and he lost all his money. He went back to his master and said, “I am sorry.” His kind master forgave him.

vocabulary.definition: A hard thing you can see through, like a window.

pages.title: The Secret of the Glass
pages.content:
They worked together again for a long time. One day, the master said, “Now you are ready. Come with me.” They went into a dark room. A little light came in through a small hole in the ceiling.

The master held a hot glass cup in the light. Inside it, there was a very small air bubble. The master blew on it, “Püf!”, and the bubble was gone.

Now the apprentice understood. “My cups broke because of the bubbles!” he said. He thanked his master and opened a very good shop. In Turkish, people call the secret of a job “püf noktası”.

vocabulary.definition: An open place in something.
The top part of a room, over your head.
A very small ball of air.
Push air out of your mouth.
A thing only a few people know.

exercises.title: Look: Two Kinds of Past
exercises.instructions: Put each verb in the right group.
exercises.question: How does each verb show the past?
exercises.explanation: Many verbs add -ed: visit → visited, check → checked. Some verbs change: teach → taught, throw → threw, break → broke, forgive → forgave.

feedback.correct: Well done. You found the two kinds of past.

exercises.question: Who is it?

matchingPairs.right: He threw the shoes on the roof.

correctAnswer.the Ahî leader: He threw the shoes on the roof.

exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: the shoemaker. Chapter 5: the Ahî leader. Chapter 6: the kind master.

feedback.incorrect: Read Chapters 4, 5 and 6 again.

exercises.title: Pabucu Dama Atılmak
exercises.question: What does “pabucu dama atılmak” mean?
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “In Turkish, people still say ‘pabucu dama atılmak’. It means ‘his shoes are on the roof’.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the last part of Chapter 5.

exercises.title: The Young Learner
exercises.question: The young learner lost all his money.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 6: “Nobody wanted his cups, and he lost all his money.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the second paragraph of Chapter 6.

exercises.title: The Dark Room
exercises.question: How did light come into the dark room?
options: through a small hole in the ceiling
exercises.explanation: Chapter 7: “A little light came in through a small hole in the ceiling.”

feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph of Chapter 7.

exercises.title: The Glass Cups
exercises.question: What happened first?

sequencingItems.text: The young learner opened a shop in a different city.
The young learner went back and said, “I am sorry.”
The master showed the young learner the air bubble.
The young learner opened a very good shop.

exercises.explanation: A shop in a different city (Chapter 6) → “I am sorry” (Chapter 6) → the bubble (Chapter 7) → a very good shop (Chapter 7).

feedback.correct: Great! You know the story of the glass cups.
feedback.incorrect: Think about the order of Chapters 6 and 7.
